list.listitem: Primary hyperhidrosis is excessive bilateral sweating either of the palms, soles, axillae, or craniofacial region for at least 6 months. C
It is important to rule out secondary causes of hyperhidrosis before beginning treatment, particularly in patients presenting later in life. C

Initial treatment of palmoplantar hyperhidrosis should include topical aluminum chloride, topical glycopyrronium tosylate, or tap water iontophoresis. If those are unsuccessful, consider botulinum toxin A (BTX-A) injections; if that fails, consider endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy. B

Initial treatment of axillary hyperhidrosis is with topical aluminum chloride. Other options include (in order): BTX-A injections and local sweat gland resection or endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy. B

background.definition: Hyperhidrosis is perspiration in excess of the physiologic amount necessary to maintain thermal homeostasis.

list.listitem: A pilot study of young Israelis reported an incidence of hyperhidrosis of 1%.
A survey of the US population found a prevalence of hyperhidrosis of 2.8%.

Primary or idiopathic hyperhidrosis is caused by an increased function of the eccrine sweat glands rather than an increased number or size. Patients with primary hyperhidrosis have higher than normal basal level of sweat production, as well as increased response to normal stimuli such as emotional or physical stress.
Most patients report a positive family history, suggesting that a genetic predisposition may exist.

There are numerous disease states that can cause secondary hyperhidrosis, which are listed in the Differential Diagnosis section. These diseases should be excluded before diagnosing a patient with primary hyperhidrosis.

There are 2 to 4 million eccrine sweat glands; these glands are more heavily concentrated on the palms, soles, axillae, and face, which explains why these regions are most commonly affected in patients with hyperhidrosis.

The thermoregulatory center in the hypothalamus controls body temperature by regulating eccrine sweat output and blood flow to the skin. This center responds not only to changes in body core temperature but also to hormones, endogenous pyrogens, physical activity, and emotions.

The sweat glands on the palms and soles appear to be activated primarily by emotional stimuli, by receiving information exclusively from the cortex, while axillary sweating is stimulated by both thermoregulatory changes and changes in emotions. Therefore, palmoplantar hyperhidrosis, unlike generalized hyperhidrosis, does not occur during sleep or sedation.

The complete pathophysiology of hyperhidrosis is not completely understood, but one of the underlying mechanisms for a lowered threshold and exaggerated response of the eccrine glands in patients with hyperhidrosis may be excessive sympathetic activity.
Visible signs of hyperhidrosis are usually clearly evident with bilateral sweating of the axillae, palms, soles, or craniofacial region that can impair daily activity. C
Hyperhidrosis usually occurs at least once a week with cessation of sweating during sleep. It usually starts before age 25 and often there is a positive family history. C
Diagnostic testing to quantify perspiration is not routinely recommended. C
Laboratory testing is recommended only when a secondary cause is suspected on the basis of the history and physical examination. C

Differential.Differential_Features: History of fever, fatigue, cough, leukocytosis, HIV infection, or sepsis
History of diabetes mellitus, gout, hyperthyroidism, or acromegaly
Experienced only during exercise, overdressing, or during menopause
History of taking propranolol, physostigmine, pilocarpine, tricyclic antidepressant, venlafaxine, antiemetics. Recent history of narcotic withdrawal
Imaging reveals intrathoracic or intracranial neoplasm (pheochromocytoma, carcinoid tumor). History of Hodgkin's disease with night sweating
History of facial surgical procedure (Frey syndrome), history of diabetes mellitus (diabetic neuropathy), history of herpes zoster or parotid abscess

list.listitem: Primary or idiopathic hyperhidrosis is defined as excess sweating for at least 6 months with at least 2 of the following characteristics: (1) bilateral, relatively symmetric sweating in the axillae, palms, soles, or craniofacial region; (2) impairment of daily activities; (3) frequency of at least 1 episode per week; (4) age of onset younger than 25 years; (5) positive family history of hyperhidrosis; and (6) cessation of focal sweating during sleep.

A disease severity scale defines sweating that is tolerable but sometimes interfering with daily activities as level 2, barely tolerable and frequently interfering with activities as level 3, and intolerable and always interfering with daily activities as level 4.

When performing an evaluation, the history should include questions about the duration and frequency of symptoms, specific triggers, amount of sweat produced, presence of sweat during sleep, areas involved, age of onset, and family history.
The social history should review alcohol and drug use.

The review of symptoms should try to exclude possible secondary causes such as endocrine disorders, infections, or malignancy (fever, weight loss, palpitations, loss of appetite, chest pain, night sweats, arthritis, or cough).

The physical examination should also try to exclude possible secondary causes (lymphadenopathy, tachycardia, tachypnea, pyrexia, evidence and location of excess sweating). Visible signs of hyperhidrosis are usually clearly evident; if direct visualization of the affected area is desired, the iodine starch test may be used.

The iodine starch test is done by applying a 2% iodine solution to the affected area and allowing it to dry. Then powdered starch is brushed on the area and as sweat is produced the light brown iodine color turns dark purple or black.
Gravimetry and evaporimetry are mostly used in research to measure the quantity of sweat being produced. Routine use of these tests is not recommended in clinical practice.

Routine laboratory evaluation is also not recommended. Diagnostic testing for secondary causes should be based on the history and physical examination. If the patient reports symptoms such as fever, weight loss, palpitations, loss of appetite, cough, chest pain, night sweats, or arthritis, then tests such as CBC, TSH, HIV testing, blood culture, urinary catecholamines, chest x-ray, PPD, or uric acid levels may be indicated.

Hyperhidrosis is a clinical diagnosis; testing to quantify perspiration is not routinely recommended. In unilateral or asymmetric hyperhidrosis, it is important to rule out a neurological lesion or malignancy.

Laboratory testing is not required if the patient presents with a characteristic presentation. However, if upon full evaluation the patient reports symptoms suggestive of a secondary cause or if symptoms begin later in life, then the appropriate testing should be ordered as indicated (see Differential Diagnosis and Diagnostic Testing sections for examples).

Topical aluminum chloride should be used as a first-line treatment and is mostly effective for mild cases of hyperhidrosis. Glycopyrronium tosylate and sofpironium may also be effective once daily topical therapies.B
Tap water iontophoresis is a good alternative first-line treatment for palmoplantar hyperhidrosis.B
Botulinum toxin A (BTX-A) is the best studied treatment for axillary or palmoplantar hyperhidrosis and is recommended when the above 2 treatment options are ineffective.B

Surgical treatments should only be used as a last resort after all other treatments have failed. Local sweat gland destruction or removal by curettage, excision, or liposuction would be considered third-line treatments if BTX-A has failed. Endothoracic sympathectomy or percutaneous thoracic phenol sympathicolysis are the last treatment options in severe hyperhidrosis; compensatory sweating after these procedures reduces patient satisfaction. B

Prescription-strength aluminum chloride hexahydrate antiperspirants, such as Drysol (20% aluminum chloride) or Xerac (6.25% aluminum tetrachloride), are thought to be effective because they produce a complex between keratin in the sweat ducts and the metal ions in the product which obstructs sweat pores and induces atrophy of the secretory cells within eccrine sweat glands. These agents are applied to dry skin nightly until clinical relief is achieved. Effects should be noted within a month, at which point the intervals between applications should be lengthened.

Glycopyrronium tosylate 3.75% is a topical anticholinergic applied once daily. It was compared with vehicle in two manufacturer sponsored RCTs with 697 patients. Patients receiving the active drug were more likely to achieve a clinically meaningful response on an 11 point symptom score of 4 or more points (59.5% vs 27.6%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).

Sofpironium topical gel 12.45% applied nightly significantly reduces sweat production and disease severity in patients 9 years and older with primary axillary hyperhidrosis, compared to placebo (NNT = 4.7). However, adverse events (eg, dry mouth, blurred vision, local irritation) leading to study withdrawal occurred more frequently in the sofpironium group (4% vs 0%).

Other preparations including tannic acid, formalin, and glutaraldehyde are not first-line agents, but can be tried as conservative alternatives to more invasive treatments if aluminum chloride is insufficient.

Anticholinergic medications such as propantheline bromide (Probanthine), glycopyrrolate (Robinul), oxybutynin (Ditropan), and benztropine (Cogentin) are effective because they inhibit the binding of acetylcholine, which is the neurotransmitter responsible for hyperhidrosis. Clinical effects usually occur within days; however, the use of these medications is very limited because of the adverse effects of mydriasis, blurry vision, dry eyes and mouth, urinary retention, and constipation. Often these severe systemic adverse effects are seen at the concentrations needed to treat hyperhidrosis, therefore these medications should only be used in severe cases. A randomized trial of 50 patients with palmar hyperhidrosis compared oxybutynin with placebo. The dose began at 2.5 mg oxybutynin once daily, increasing to 5 mg twice daily after 6 weeks. The treatment was effective and well tolerated at this dose.
A randomized placebo controlled trial in 62 patients showed oxybutynin from 2.5 to 7.5 mg daily was superior to placebo for hyperhidrosis severity (p = 0.009) and improved quality of life scores.

β-blockers and benzodiazepines may be helpful in patients with hyperhidrosis related to specific emotional events; however, these should be used on a limited basis (before a specific stressful situation) because of the potential for dependency and side effects such as lethargy.

BTX-A is approved for the treatment of axillary hyperhidrosis, and is effective for palmoplantar and facial hyperhidrosis, as well. BTX-A intradermal injections inhibit the release of acetylcholine from presynaptic nerve endings, blocking the sympathetic cholinergic autonomic fibers that innervate sweat glands. The injections are placed 1.5 cm apart over the affected area. Efficacy can be observed within a week and the duration of anhidrosis varies from 4 to 13 months.
A systematic review of 23 studies including 10 RCTs concluded that the drug was consistently effective and safe, but did not perform meta-analysis.
Surgical excision or SC liposuction of the affected area, surgical sympathectomy, and percutaneous thoracic phenol sympathicolysis have all been used effectively to treat hyperhidrosis.

However, surgical excision or SC liposuction can result in compensatory sweating and other surgical complications. Therefore, these treatments should only be used if all other options have been unsuccessful.

An expert consensus guideline from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons recommended endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy (ETS) as the best therapy, using either relectrocautery or clipping. They report the best success rates when interruption is at the top of the 3rd rib (or at the top of the 4th rib for palmar only hyperhidrosis). They recommend interruption as the top of R3 for craniofacial hyperhidrosis.

T4 endothoracic sympathectomy is safe and effective with long-term improvement in quality of life. However, compensatory sweating affected 24% (severe 7%) at 5-year follow-up. More specific T2 and T3 sympathectomy for palmar hyperhidrosis may have less compensatory sweating.

T4 compared to T3 thoracic sympathectomy for palmar hyperhidrosis was reviewed in 629 patients (T4) and 566 patients (T3) and was associated with a lower incidence of postoperative compensatory sweating, dry hands, and gustatory sweating in T4 patients. No significant difference in symptom resolution or patient satisfaction was found between the groups.
Fractionated microneedle radiofrequency is another minimally invasive surgical treatment option for axillary hyperhidrosis.

Iontophoresis is useful for palmarplantar hyperhidrosis, but is difficult to administer to the axillary area. The physician (or the patient himself) uses a battery-powered device to deliver a low current of electricity to hands and feet while the patient's body is immersed in water.

A randomized, sham-controlled single blind study treated 27 patients with palmar hyperhidrosis with tap water iontophoresis. After 10 treatments there was clinical improvement in 92.9% patients receiving active iontophoresis compared to 38.5% (sham treatment) (p = 0.001). The mean sweat secretion rate was reduced by 92% compared to 39% (p <0.001) with improvement in quality of life in 79% compared to 31% (p = 0.028).

The Drionic is a battery-operated machine available commercially with a prescription. There is a unit that can be used to treat the palms and soles, as well as a separate unit to treat the axillae. Six to twelve 30-minute treatments usually produce the desired effect, after which maintenance therapy can be administered weekly or monthly.
Another treatment option for axillary hyperhidrosis is local microwave therapy.
Topical medications need to be constantly applied; after they become effective, however, the frequency may be reduced. C
BTX-A needs to be repeated every 4 to 12 months. A
The only possibility of permanent treatment is surgery, but surgery may cause compensatory sweating, as well as other serious surgical complications. B
